items.title: Reframing Homer's Sirens through gender, nature and social order
items.summary: Though they are pivotal to Homer's epic, luring Odysseus with the promise of eternal wisdom, the Greek poet barely described the mysterious Sirens. What might a better understanding of these formless, disembodied feminine creatures contribute to this timeless teaching myth?

items.title: How chromosomes find their partners
items.summary: For a long time, so-called satellite DNA was considered largely worthless. Now, ETH Zurich researchers have shown in fruit flies that these repetitive sections of genetic material act as a kind of barcode, enabling the correct chromosomes to recognize one another.

items.title: Scientists identify design rules for the best thermoelectric materials
items.summary: Researchers from Tokyo Metropolitan University have used a theoretical framework to derive design rules for creating new thermoelectric materials. items.title: GenAI cannot accurately grade student essays in higher education, study finds
items.summary: New research from Cardiff University and the University of Melbourne has investigated whether GenAI could mimic human marking when evaluating written student work. The results have been published in the journal Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education.

items.title: New free-space optical link adds a wireless component to the nation's longest quantum network
items.summary: There's a new lighthouse on Long Island. But instead of shining light to guide ships through waterways, this one transmits and receives particles of light that carry quantum information. items.title: Long-term study reveals hidden threat of schistosomiasis in endangered chimpanzees
items.summary: A 12-year study of rescued chimpanzees at the Ngamba Island Chimpanzee Sanctuary (NICS) in Uganda has revealed persistent intestinal schistosomiasis infections, highlighting the need for long-term disease surveillance to protect endangered wildlife.

items.title: Dry landscapes and newly fallowed fields may raise California Valley fever risk
items.summary: Researchers at UC San Diego and UC Berkeley have found that certain landscapes surrounding California communities are associated with differing rates of Valley fever, a fungal respiratory infection caused by inhaling spores carried in windblown dust.

items.title: Immigration can bring small overall gains but uneven wage effects
items.summary: Immigration can produce a small economic gain for the native-born population overall while causing larger shifts in wages between different groups of workers, according to new research co-authored by King's Business School.

items.title: Common medications may change your gut for years
items.summary: Common medications may reshape the gut microbiome long after the last dose is taken. items.summary: Astronomers have found a four-star system doing something that has never been confirmed before. The system, TIC 433545934, has two close pairs of stars orbiting each other. items.title: How to CT scan a 400-pound crocodile
items.summary: At 61, Bill had begun showing changes in his health—decreased appetite, weight loss and abdominal bloating. But his bloodwork was normal, leaving the cause of his symptoms unknown. items.title: Australia's bird flu response: Too little, but it's not too late
items.summary: When news broke over the weekend that Australia's first mainland case of bird flu in a mammal—the death of a long-nosed fur seal—had been detected, I felt deep sadness and dread for what's likely to come next. We should expect large-scale deaths of mammals, in addition to birds.

items.title: Bird flu is spreading. Your backyard feeder could make it worse
items.summary: Backyard bird feeders could become unexpected hotspots for H5N1 as Australia’s bird flu outbreak spreads, bringing species together in ways that rarely occur naturally. Experts say stopping feeding is safest, while smaller amounts of food, no hand-feeding, and careful cleaning can reduce the danger.

items.title: An AI job boom? Here's what the tedious, temporary work in data labeling is actually like
items.summary: Amid all the talk about artificial intelligence (AI) both creating and destroying jobs, a troubling reality flies under the radar.

items.title: Why hundreds of scientists want more protection for Australia's oceans
items.summary: Australia is one of the world's great ocean nations. It is home to more marine species than any other country, with ocean ecosystems spanning all five of the world's climate zones, from the coral-rich tropics to the icy shores of Antarctica.

items.title: A ghostly ribbon of stars reveals hidden dark matter
items.summary: A faint ribbon of stars around a distant galaxy has become the first globular cluster stellar stream ever identified beyond the Milky Way. items.title: A tiny “rainbow on a chip” could help supercharge 6G networks
items.summary: Researchers have created a tiny chip that produces a stable “rainbow” of light capable of generating multiple high-frequency signals at once, potentially boosting the speed and capacity of future 6G networks. items.title: Book Week is not just for big kids—how to engage babies and toddlers at story time
items.summary: Book Week is a great opportunity for parents and caregivers to inspire a love of reading in babies and toddlers.

items.title: Housing may shape death risks for low-income older renters
items.summary: For low-income older adults, where they live may affect how long they live, according to new research from Washington University in St. Louis.

items.title: Too much or too little sleep may make your body age faster
items.summary: Both too little and too much sleep may be linked to faster aging throughout the body. Researchers analyzing 23 biological aging clocks found the lowest aging levels among people sleeping about 6.4 to 7.8 hours per day. items.title: Recycling meat waste may help bring cultivated meat to market
items.summary: Researchers found microalgae can be grown using waste from cultivated meat production, then processed and fed back into the system, replacing some of the expensive ingredients needed to grow new meat cells.

items.title: Study finds food insecurity remains in historically redlined neighborhoods

items.title: Screen time at ages 1 and 6 may matter more than parents realize
items.summary: More screen time during infancy and around the start of school was linked to poorer academic performance and weaker working memory years later. The findings suggest that early childhood may contain particularly sensitive windows when screen habits can have longer-lasting effects.

items.title: Scientists just imaged the hidden quantum shape of a molecule
items.summary: Researchers have found a way to create a complete 3D image of a molecule’s wavefunction, one of quantum mechanics’ most fundamental yet elusive features. items.title: Engineered yeasts help turn PET plastic and crop waste into protein-rich cookies
items.summary: Plastic might be the last ingredient you would ever add to a cookie recipe. But a team of researchers is looking to change that. items.title: Nanoparticle flu vaccine protects against three influenza strains in mice
items.summary: A new nanoparticle vaccine could one day give patients immunity to the flu with fewer trips to the doctor and without requiring health officials to correctly guess which flu strains will become dominant each year.

items.title: China says unmanned moon mission delayed over 'launch conditions'
items.summary: China's manned space agency said Sunday it is delaying a research moon mission that is part of Beijing's efforts to land a crew there by 2030, less than two weeks after a rare launch failure.

items.title: Fizičari prvi put uočili kvantne toplinske valove na sobnoj temperaturi
items.summary: FIZIČARI su prvi put uočili kvantno ponašanje toplinskih valova na sobnoj temperaturi. Otkriće, postignuto s borovim arsenidom, omogućuje precizniju kontrolu topline u kvantnoj elektronici.

items.title: NASA is about to launch a powerful new eye on the universe
items.summary: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has been cleared for final launch preparations ahead of a targeted August 30 liftoff aboard SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy. The powerful new observatory will probe cosmic expansion, the history of the universe, and distant exoplanets.

items.title: Trump to award Congressional Space Medal of Honor to Artemis II astronauts
items.summary: The Artemis II crew will receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor after becoming the first humans in more than 50 years to travel beyond the Moon. Their 10-day Orion mission also carried them farther into space than anyone in history.

items.title: What Lake Bonneville Left Behind
items.summary: The drying of the massive lake exposed playas that became the setting for feats of engineering and technological ingenuity, as well as epic tales of exploration and desperation.

items.title: Scientists discover a real-life “dragon” and name it after Syrax
items.summary: Scientists discovered a small, yellowish mountain horned dragon in Thailand and named it Acanthosaura syrax after a dragon from House of the Dragon. Found only in a narrow band of high-elevation forest, the distinctive new species could become a flagship for protecting its rare mountain habitat.

items.title: Gut bacteria may unlock a hidden benefit of vegetables
items.summary: Gut bacteria can transform nitrate and plant-based iron from vegetables and other foods into protective molecules that may benefit the heart and metabolism. items.summary: Humans develop at a slower rate than other mammalian species, like mice, but scientists are still trying to understand the molecular basis of these differences. items.title: Could teaching assistants be an overlooked teacher pipeline? New research says yes
items.summary: As school districts continue searching for ways to recruit and retain teachers, new research from UNC-Chapel Hill suggests one promising pipeline may already be in classrooms: teaching assistants.

items.title: Collaborative drawing offers new insights into how strangers become friends
items.summary: The closer two people grow, the more alike their brains work—or so the assumption goes. items.title: Oldest human brain cells grown in lab 'recorded passage of time'
items.summary: Peppercorn-sized clumps of human brain cells grown in a lab for a record seven years aged similarly to those inside our heads, suggesting they "recorded the passage of time," scientists said Wednesday.

items.summary: SVJETLOST štednih žarulja utječe na razne funkcije organizma.

items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a possible reason why the Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 can disrupt the brain long before memory problems begin. items.summary: An abandoned farm field became a flourishing wildflower meadow within little more than a decade, with plant diversity doubling and thousands of orchids appearing naturally. items.summary: Of Jupiter's four Galilean moons, Callisto is the one that gets the least attention. Io is constantly being resurfaced by volcanoes. Europa has a giant liquid water ocean. items.summary: Blue morpho butterflies have captivated the human eye for centuries. We even have one as an emoji on our phones. items.title: China abruptly postpones ambitious Chang'e-7 lunar mission launch
items.summary: China said on Sunday it was postponing its planned ambitious Chang'e-7 lunar mission, which was set to carry out explorations including searching for water ice on the moon.

items.title: The dental crown of the future could be 3D-printed while you wait
items.summary: Researchers have found a way to slash the processing time for 3D-printed zirconia crowns from as much as 100 hours to under 30 minutes. The advance could eventually let dentists print strong, customized permanent crowns for patients within a single appointment.
